en: Rough and bad-mannered; rude and insensitive
hook: BOORISH: like a BOAR (wild pig) at the dinner table.
story: Boorish. At the most expensive restaurant in Gulshan, one guest talked loudly on speakerphone, chewed with his mouth wide open, wiped his hands on the tablecloth, and snapped his fingers at the waiters. When the food arrived, he complained in a voice the whole room could hear. Diners at other tables stared in disbelief. His behaviour was boorish: rough, rude, and insensitive to others. A boor has no social grace, like a wild boar at a dinner party.

gre.s: The guest's ____ behavior at the formal dinner, including shouting across the table and mocking the host, embarrassed everyone present.
gre.clue: shouting across the table and mocking the host

en: To tolerate or allow (usually used in the negative)
hook: GRE trick: BROOK isn't just a stream. 'She brooks no nonsense' means she TOLERATES none.
story: Brook. On her first day, the new headmistress made one rule clear: lateness would not be tolerated. Five minutes late, and you waited outside until break, whether you were a student or a teacher. A senior teacher arrived late on day two and tried to explain. She held up one hand. "I brook no excuses." To brook means to tolerate or allow, and it almost always appears with no or not. Most students think brook only means a small stream.

gre.s: The editor was famous for her exacting standards and would ____ no errors, however minor, in the articles she approved.
gre.clue: famous for her exacting standards

en: Cautious; carefully considering all circumstances before acting
hook: CIRCUM-SPECT: looking (spect) all around (circum) before acting.
story: Circumspect. Before signing the lease for her first flat, Nadia read every clause twice, called the landlord's previous tenants, checked the water pressure in every tap, inspected the wiring, and asked a lawyer friend to review the contract. Her friends teased her for being paranoid. A year later, while their landlords cheated them, Nadia had no problems at all. She was circumspect: cautious, carefully considering every circumstance before acting. Circum means around, spect means look.

gre.s: Having been burned by a previous scandal, the senator was ____ in her public statements, weighing every word before she spoke.
gre.clue: weighing every word before she spoke

en: Courteous and considerate behavior; mutual respect between groups or nations
hook: COMITY looks like COMMUNITY: people living in harmony.
story: Comity. In the old neighbourhood of Lalbagh, Muslim, Hindu, Christian, and Buddhist families have lived side by side for generations. During Eid, Hindu neighbours receive plates of semai. During Puja, Muslim children watch the processions. At Christmas, everyone gets cake. Disagreements are settled over tea. This harmony is called comity: courteous, considerate behaviour and mutual respect between groups or nations. It looks like community, and it describes a community at its best.

gre.s: Despite fierce competition in the market, the two firms maintained a surprising ____, regularly sharing research and referring clients to each other.
gre.clue: regularly sharing research and referring clients to each other

en: Corresponding in size, degree, or amount; proportionate
hook: COM-MEASURE-ate: of the same MEASURE.
story: Commensurate. Arif worked eighty hours a week: weekends, holidays, nights. He trained new staff and fixed every crisis. Yet his salary was the same as colleagues who left at five. One day he walked into his manager's office and said, "I would like a salary commensurate with my responsibilities." Commensurate means corresponding in size or degree; proportionate. Com means with, mensurate means measure. A punishment should be commensurate with the crime.

gre.s: Applicants will be offered a salary ____ with their experience, so senior candidates can expect considerably higher pay.
gre.clue: so senior candidates can expect considerably higher pay

en: Warm, friendly, and polite
hook: CORDIAL: from the HEART (cor, as in cardiac).
story: Cordial. Everyone expected the two rival company owners to glare at each other at the business conference. Instead, they shook hands warmly, asked about each other's families, and shared a table at lunch, laughing about old times. They competed fiercely in the market but respected each other personally. Their relationship was cordial: warm, friendly, and polite. Cor means heart, as in cardiac. A cordial invitation comes sincerely from the heart.

gre.s: Though the negotiations were tense, relations between the two delegations remained ____, and each side thanked the other warmly at the close.
gre.clue: each side thanked the other warmly

en: Causing harm or damage
hook: DELETE-rious: it DELETES your health.
story: Deleterious. In some villages in Bangladesh, the water from tube wells looks clean and tastes fine. But tests revealed arsenic, a poison with no colour and no smell. Over years, people who drank it developed skin lesions, cancers, and slow damage to their organs. The arsenic was deleterious: harmful and damaging. Think: it deletes your health. Smoking is deleterious to the lungs; sleepless nights are deleterious to memory.

gre.s: Researchers found that even small amounts of the chemical have ____ effects on the nervous system, especially in children.
gre.clue: especially in children

en: A division or contrast between two opposing things
hook: DI-CHOTOMY: cutting in two (di = two, tomy = cut).
story: Dichotomy. The documentary opened with a single shot from a drone above Dhaka. On one side of the lake: glittering towers, rooftop pools, and luxury cars in Gulshan. On the other side: tin-roofed slums packed with families of eight in single rooms. Rich and poor, separated only by a strip of water. A dichotomy is a sharp division or contrast between two opposing things. Di means two, tomy means cut. GRE passages often criticize false dichotomies.

gre.s: The author rejects the traditional ____ between reason and emotion, arguing that the two are deeply intertwined in every decision.
gre.clue: arguing that the two are deeply intertwined

en: To instruct or improve someone morally or intellectually
hook: EDIFY: builds you up like an EDIFICE (building).
story: Edify. Every evening during load-shedding, Grandfather lit a lantern and told the children stories. A greedy king who lost everything. A poor boy who returned a lost wallet. A girl who studied by candlelight and became a doctor. The stories entertained them, but they also quietly taught honesty, patience, and courage. Grandfather meant to edify: to improve someone morally or intellectually. An edifying documentary teaches you something valuable. Edify shares a root with edifice: it builds you up.

gre.s: The museum's new exhibits are designed to ____ as well as entertain, teaching visitors about climate science through interactive games.
gre.clue: teaching visitors about climate science

en: Well chosen or suited to the situation; pleasing and fortunate
hook: FELICITOUS: FELICITY = happiness. A happily perfect choice.
story: Felicitous. At the farewell party for her favourite teacher, Mitu stood up and quoted one line from Tagore about a boat setting out on a river toward a new shore. It fit the moment so perfectly that the teacher, who was retiring after forty years, wiped tears from her eyes. Mitu's choice was felicitous: perfectly suited to the situation, pleasing and well timed. Felicity means happiness. A felicitous phrase fits like a key in a lock.

gre.s: The editor praised the translator's ____ choice of words, which captured the original poem's music without sacrificing its meaning.
gre.clue: captured the original poem's music without sacrificing its meaning

en: Having or showing great knowledge gained from study
hook: ERUDITE: 'E-READ-ITE', someone who has read everything.
story: Erudite. Professor Rahman can discuss Bengali poetry, Greek philosophy, quantum physics, and Mughal architecture in a single conversation, quoting books from memory and connecting ideas across centuries. Students joke that he has read every book in the library twice. He is erudite: having great knowledge gained from deep study. Think: e-read-ite, a person who has read everything. An erudite essay is full of learning. Synonyms: scholarly, learned.

gre.s: Although the lecture was ____, packed with references to obscure philosophers, the speaker made it accessible to a general audience.
gre.clue: packed with references to obscure philosophers

en: Very fertile; capable of producing abundantly; intellectually productive
hook: FECUND: FERTILE and fruitful; produces a FECUND harvest.
story: Fecund. Every monsoon, the great rivers of Bangladesh flood their banks and leave behind a thick layer of fresh silt. When the water recedes, farmers plant immediately, and the land produces three rice harvests a year. The delta is one of the most fecund regions on Earth: extremely fertile and productive. Fecund is also used for minds. A fecund imagination produces endless creative ideas. Think: fertile and fruitful.

gre.s: The novelist's ____ imagination produced more than forty books in two decades, each populated by dozens of memorable characters.
gre.clue: produced more than forty books in two decades

en: Lacking physical strength; weak and unconvincing
hook: FEEBLE: sounds weak, like a FEEBLE 'meh'.
story: Feeble. After two weeks of dengue fever, Tanvir's grandfather was so feeble that he could not lift a glass of water. Tanvir held it to his lips. That same week, Tanvir missed an assignment deadline and told his professor that his dog had eaten his laptop. He does not have a dog. The professor sighed at such a feeble excuse. Feeble means lacking physical strength, or weak and unconvincing. A feeble attempt barely tries.

gre.s: The company's ____ response to the crisis, a single vague press release issued a week late, only deepened customers' anger.
gre.clue: a single vague press release issued a week late

en: To refrain from doing something; to hold back
hook: FOR-BEAR: BEAR (endure) it FOR now, and hold yourself back.
story: Forbear. At the Eid dinner, Sara's aunt said loudly, "Still not married? And so thin!" Sara felt the words rising in her throat. She wanted to tell her aunt exactly what she thought. Instead, she took a slow breath, smiled, and passed the rice. She forbore, for the sake of family peace. To forbear is to hold yourself back from doing or saying something. Do not confuse it with forebear, which means an ancestor.

gre.s: Though provoked repeatedly by the hecklers, the speaker managed to ____ from responding and simply continued his talk.
gre.clue: simply continued his talk

en: Lacking order or plan; random
hook: HAP-HAZARD: by HAPpenstance and HAZARD, by chance.
story: Haphazard. Imran's study method: ten words from group nine, then a geometry video, then an essay, then back to group two, then a snack, then reading comprehension, then group nine again. No schedule. No pattern. No plan. After a month he had studied a little of everything and learned almost nothing. His approach was haphazard: lacking order or planning, random. Hap means chance, as in happen. Haphazard construction leads to unsafe buildings.

gre.s: Because the samples were collected in a ____ manner, with no consistent procedure, the study's conclusions cannot be trusted.
gre.clue: with no consistent procedure

en: A confused mixture of different things
hook: HODGEPODGE: in Bangla, it's literally a 'khichuri' of things.
story: Hodgepodge. Zayan's bedroom contained: two cricket bats, a broken guitar, five GRE books, a fish tank without any fish, a bicycle wheel, twelve unmatched socks, a trophy from 2014, and a model of the solar system missing Jupiter. His mother called it a museum of nonsense. It was a hodgepodge: a confused mixture of unrelated things. In Bangla, you might call it a khichuri, where everything gets thrown into one pot.

gre.s: Rather than presenting a coherent theory, the book offers a ____ of anecdotes, statistics, and speculation loosely stitched together.
gre.clue: loosely stitched together

en: To slow down or block progress
hook: IM-PEDE: 'ped' is foot. Something catching your feet.
story: Impede. On the morning of her GRE, Mitu left home two hours early. Then the rain started. Streets flooded knee-deep. Her bus broke down. A protest blocked the main road. A rickshaw chain snapped. Everything seemed to impede her journey: slow it down or block it. She arrived with four minutes to spare. To impede is to obstruct or hinder progress. Ped means foot, as in pedal: something catching your feet. An impediment is an obstacle.

gre.s: Heavy snowfall continued to ____ the rescue effort, preventing helicopters from reaching the stranded climbers for three days.
gre.clue: preventing helicopters from reaching the stranded climbers

en: Acting quickly without careful thought
hook: IMPETUOUS: full of IMPETUS (sudden force), no brakes.
story: Impetuous. During a heated argument with his boss about a project deadline, Farhan slammed his laptop shut and shouted, "I quit!" He walked out, feeling powerful. By the evening, he felt sick. He had no savings, no other job, and a family depending on him. His decision had been impetuous: made quickly, on impulse, without careful thought. Impetus means sudden force. Impetuous people act first and think later.

gre.s: The general's ____ decision to attack before reinforcements arrived, made in a moment of anger, cost him the battle.
gre.clue: made in a moment of anger

en: Easily angered; hot-tempered
hook: IRASCIBLE: quick to IRE (anger).
story: Irascible. Old Mr. Karim runs a stationery shop near the school. Ask him a question twice, and he shouts. Touch a pen without buying it, and he snaps. Pay with a large note, and he grumbles for five minutes. Children dare each other to go in. He is irascible: easily angered, hot-tempered. Ira is Latin for anger, as in irate. An irascible person is like a firecracker with a very short fuse.

gre.s: The ____ conductor was notorious for exploding at musicians over the slightest mistake, once storming out of a rehearsal over a single wrong note.
gre.clue: exploding at musicians over the slightest mistake

en: Motivated only by money; a soldier hired to fight for a foreign army
hook: MERCENARY: works only for MERCHANDISE and money.
story: Mercenary. Patients at one private clinic noticed something strange. Every patient, whatever their illness, was told they needed expensive tests, scans, and often surgery. The doctor's bank balance grew, but his patients did not get better. A journalist finally exposed him. He was mercenary: motivated purely by money, not by care for others. Historically, mercenaries were soldiers hired to fight for whichever ruler paid them most. Think: works only for merchandise.

gre.s: Critics charged that the consultant's advice was ____, designed less to help her clients than to maximize her own fees.
gre.clue: designed less to help her clients than to maximize her own fees

en: Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise
hook: METICULOUS: METIC-ulous, every metric measured perfectly.
story: Meticulous. Before every exam, half of Joya's class lines up to borrow her notes. Each page is colour-coded: blue for definitions, green for examples, red for exceptions. Every diagram is labelled. Every margin holds a summary. There is not a single crossed-out word. Her notes are meticulous: showing extreme care and attention to detail. A meticulous surgeon leaves nothing to chance. Synonyms: scrupulous, painstaking, punctilious.

gre.s: The restoration took six years because the conservators were ____, cleaning the fresco one square centimeter at a time.
gre.clue: cleaning the fresco one square centimeter at a time

en: Sharply sarcastic or critical
hook: MORDANT: it BITES (Latin mordere, to bite).
story: Mordant. The comedian on the late-night show was famous for his mordant humour. He described a minister's new policy as "a solution looking for a problem" and a celebrity's memoir as "three hundred pages of mirrors." The audience laughed and winced at the same time. Mordant means sharply sarcastic and biting. In Latin, mordere means to bite. A mordant critic's words sting long after you have stopped laughing. Synonyms: caustic, acerbic.

gre.s: The columnist's ____ wit spared no one, and politicians dreaded seeing their names in her biting weekly column.
gre.clue: politicians dreaded seeing their names in her biting weekly column

en: To move faster than; to exceed or surpass
hook: OUT-STRIP: running OUT ahead on the race STRIP.
story: Outstrip. When Dhaka's first metro line opened, everyone wanted to try it. Within a week, the number of passengers outstripped every prediction. Platforms overflowed, and extra trains had to be added. Demand had outstripped supply: exceeded it, raced past it. To outstrip is to move faster than, or to surpass. A brilliant student may quickly outstrip her teachers. When spending outstrips income, debt follows. Picture a runner pulling away on the track.

gre.s: Within a decade, the small startup had come to ____ its older rivals, overtaking them in both revenue and market share.
gre.clue: overtaking them in both revenue and market share

en: Dangerously unstable or uncertain
hook: PRECARIOUS: like a CAR parked on the edge of a cliff.
story: Precarious. On a new building site in Mirpur, a construction worker stood on a thin bamboo pole six floors up, balancing a load of bricks on his head. He wore no harness, no helmet, and rubber sandals. Below him, cars honked on the busy road. One slip, one gust of wind, and he would fall. His position was precarious: dangerously unstable and uncertain. A precarious job could vanish tomorrow. Picture a car parked on a cliff edge.

gre.s: With only a single seat separating the two parties, the governing coalition's majority remained ____, liable to collapse with one defection.
gre.clue: liable to collapse with one defection

en: Having unusual or peculiar habits or features
hook: QUIRKY: full of QUIRKS, odd little habits.
story: Quirky. Mitu's new roommate eats rice with a spoon, names her plants after famous scientists, studies only while standing on one leg, and keeps a diary written entirely in emojis. On Fridays she wears a hat shaped like a fish. Mitu was confused at first; now she adores her. Her roommate is quirky: full of odd but charming little habits. A quirk is a peculiarity. A quirky café might have books hanging from the ceiling.

gre.s: Fans love the director's ____ films, which feature talking furniture, symmetrical sets, and characters who speak only in rhyme.
gre.clue: talking furniture, symmetrical sets, and characters who speak only in rhyme

en: To refuse to accept or be associated with; to reject
hook: REPUDIATE: REPEL and DENY.
story: Repudiate. A video from fifteen years ago surfaced online: a famous politician making cruel jokes about poor people. Within hours, millions had shared it. The next morning he held a press conference. "Those views were wrong. I reject them completely, and I am ashamed of them." He had repudiated his past words: refused to accept or be associated with them. Repudiate means to reject firmly. A government may also repudiate a debt, refusing to pay it.

gre.s: Hoping to save his career, the candidate was quick to ____ the extremist group that had endorsed him, insisting he shared none of its views.
gre.clue: insisting he shared none of its views

en: Skill in dealing with people without offending them
hook: TACT: a gentle TACTILE touch with words.
story: Tact. Sara's best friend came back from the salon with a bright green haircut. "Do you like it? Be honest!" Sara thought it looked like a parrot. Instead she said, "It is so bold! The colour really brings out your eyes." It was true, and her friend beamed. That is tact: skill in handling people and delicate situations without offending them. Tactless people blurt out whatever they think. Think: a gentle tactile touch with words.

gre.s: The ambassador's ____ in handling the dispute, defusing tensions without insulting either party, won her praise from both governments.
gre.clue: defusing tensions without insulting either party

en: Unimportant or trivial
hook: TRIFLE: a small, unimportant thing.
story: Trifling. At the vegetable market, a customer and a shopkeeper argued loudly for twenty minutes. A crowd gathered. Voices rose. Someone called a policeman. The cause of the fight? Two taka of change. Both men lost far more in time, energy, and dignity than the money was worth. The amount was trifling: of little value or importance. A trifle is a small, unimportant thing. Do not let trifling matters distract you from real goals.

gre.s: Although the fine was ____, a mere ten dollars, the principle at stake led the activist to appeal all the way to the supreme court.
gre.clue: a mere ten dollars

en: Characterized by conflict, disorder, or violent movement
hook: TURBULENT: like airplane TURBULENCE, shaking and chaotic.
story: Turbulent. Halfway across the Bay of Bengal, the plane hit a storm. The seatbelt sign flashed. Cups slid off trays. The cabin dropped suddenly, and passengers screamed and gripped their armrests. Twenty minutes later, the sky was calm again. The flight had been turbulent: full of violent, disordered movement. History can be turbulent too: decades full of wars, revolutions, and upheaval. Think of aeroplane turbulence: shaking, chaotic, and unpredictable.

gre.s: The country's ____ history, marked by frequent coups and civil unrest, makes its recent decade of stability all the more remarkable.
gre.clue: marked by frequent coups and civil unrest
